title: Pericles' Funeral Oration
text:
In the winter of 431 to 430 BC, after the first year of the Peloponnesian War against Sparta, Athens held its traditional public funeral for the citizens who had died in battle. The bones of the dead were carried in cypress coffins, one for each tribe, and buried in the public cemetery outside the walls. The city chose Pericles, its leading statesman, to give the speech.

The version recorded by the historian Thucydides is not mainly about the dead. Pericles spoke instead about the city they had died for. He described a democracy in which power was in the hands of the many, where people were advanced by merit rather than class, where citizens were free in their private lives yet obeyed the laws, and where people loved beauty without extravagance and wisdom without softness. Athens, he said, was an education to Greece.

Only then did he turn to the fallen, saying they had made the city's greatness their own, and to the families, offering comfort and practical advice.

Thucydides follows the speech immediately with the plague that struck Athens the next summer, which killed a large part of the population. Pericles himself died of it in 429 BC.
lesson: People bear sacrifice better when they understand what it is for. A leader's job includes saying clearly what is worth defending.
source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 2, chapters 34 to 46
caveat: Thucydides admits his speeches give the general sense of what was said, not the exact words.
